articles.title: Lula: Dívida pública preocupa e solução é crescimento econômico | G1
articles.standfirst: Entrevista à Globo, para a jornalista Renata Lo Prete, faz parte da cobertura do segundo turno das eleições presidenciais de 2026, que terá também conversa com Flávio Bolsonaro e debate entre os dois candidatos.
articles.summary: Em entrevista à Globo, Lula afirma que o crescimento da economia é o caminho para reduzir a dívida pública sem prejudicar a população mais pobre.
articles.body:
O presidente e candidato à reeleição Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) afirmou, em entrevista à Globo nesta quinta-feira (15) , que está preocupado com o crescimento da dívida pública e defendeu que a solução para o problema fiscal brasileiro é estimular o crescimento da economia, em vez de cortar gastos que afetem a população mais pobre.

“Você acha que eu não estou preocupado? Eu estou preocupado. Eu criei uma família com cinco filhos. Eu sei o que é dívida”, declarou.

A declaração foi dada à jornalista Renata Lo Prete após Lula ser questionado sobre a política de juros do Banco Central, comandado por Gabriel Galípolo, indicado por ele, e sobre a avaliação do presidente do BC de que o modelo de crescimento baseado no estímulo ao consumo estaria esgotado.

O presidente respondeu que, historicamente, as tentativas de ajuste fiscal acabam prejudicando a população de baixa renda.

“O jeito de você resolver o problema fiscal é fazer a economia ficar crescendo”, afirmou Lula. “Eu estou com 80 anos de idade, eu vivo isso há 50 anos, dessa briga: toda vez que alguém quer resolver o problema fiscal, o povo pobre paga. Toda vez, é o povo pobre. Eu não quero que o povo pague”, disse.

Lula também citou os resultados econômicos de seus primeiros mandatos para defender sua posição. Segundo ele, o crescimento da economia permitiu ao Brasil quitar a dívida com o Fundo Monetário Internacional (FMI), acumular reservas internacionais e melhorar sua posição entre as maiores economias do mundo.

“Porque o único jeito de você fazer o déficit, com relação à dívida, diminuir é crescer a economia, [e não] cortar [do] pobre”, afirmou.

Questionado sobre o aumento da dívida pública em seu atual governo e as críticas de economistas à trajetória do endividamento, Lula reconheceu a importância do controle das contas.

“Eu sei o que é dívida. Eu sei que, se a gente perdeu o controle do nosso orçamento, a coisa quebra e vai quebrar do lado mais fraco”, declarou.

O presidente afirmou ainda que tem divergências com economistas sobre a condução da política econômica e defendeu políticas de crédito e incentivo à microeconomia para “fazer o dinheiro rodar na mão do povo”.

Ao ser perguntado se pretendia mudar a condução da política econômica em um eventual novo mandato, respondeu: “Estou propondo não cortar dinheiro dos pobres”.

Lula dá entrevista ao JN — Foto: Manuella Mello/Globo

articles.standfirst: Pesquisa foi encomendada pelo jornal Folha de S.Paulo. Margem de erro é de 2 pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos.
articles.summary: Pesquisa foi encomendada pelo jornal Folha de S.Paulo. Margem de erro é de 2 pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Datafolha divulgada nesta quinta-feira (15) mostra que 46% dos eleitores entrevistados dizem rejeitar Lula (PT), e 44% rejeitam Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

Datafolha, 2º turno: rejeição — Foto: Arte/g1

Em relação à pesquisa anterior, de uma semana atrás, a rejeição de Lula ficou no mesmo patamar, e a de Flávio oscilou um ponto para cima, de 43% para 44%.

O Datafolha ouviu 2.520 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais, entre os dias 13 e 14 de outubro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. O número de registro da pesquisa na Justiça Eleitoral é BR-00466/2026.

O Datafolha mostra também que, a dez dias do 2º turno, Flávio Bolsonaro tem 47% das intenções de voto, contra 45% de Lula . Os dois candidatos estão em empate técnico dentro da margem de erro.

Em votos válidos, que excluem brancos, nulos e indecisos, Flávio Bolsonaro tem 51% e Lula, 49%. O número de votos válidos é o que a Justiça Eleitoral usa para determinar os resultados das eleições.

Em relação à pesquisa anterior, Flávio Bolsonaro oscilou dois pontos para baixo, de 49% para 47%, e Lula manteve 45%. A diferença entre eles era de quatro pontos há uma semana, e agora é de dois pontos.

articles.title: Judge tosses ex-CIA head John Brennan's document preservation lawsuit against the Justice Department
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Thursday rejected a lawsuit from John Brennan that sought to force the Justice Department to preserve investigative reco...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Thursday rejected a lawsuit from John Brennan that sought to force the Justice Department to preserve investigative records so that the former CIA director can challenge any eventual criminal case against him as a selective and malicious prosecution.

A lawyer for Brennan conceded during arguments last month that the request for a court order was unusual but said it was necessary given what he called the Justice Department's pattern of vindictiveness in its pursuit of Brennan and its recent track record of erasing or failing to preserve communications and records in other matters.

The lawsuit contends that the records being sought would demonstrate that any prosecution of Brennan, who has been investigated for months by the Trump administration Justice Department but not charged, is the product of a political vendetta to punish one of President Donald Trump's perceived adversaries.

But U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb denied Brennan's request, saying his arguments were too speculative at the moment and that the former CIA director had not proven that the Justice Department was failing to preserve records relevant to a future malicious prosecution argument.

"Brennan's allegations — that he is being targeted by the Trump Administration not because of his conduct, but because he has opposed the current president — are deeply concerning," Cobb wrote in dismissing the lawsuit. "If he was eventually able to prove those allegations true, that would certainly suggest that his potential prosecution is vindictive. But even taking all of Brennan's allegations to be truthful at this stage, the injury he alleges is simply too attenuated from the actions he seeks to enjoin to warrant a finding of standing here."

Lawyers for Brennan said in a statement that Cobb's decision addressed a technical matter of legal standing and was not based on their argument "that the Justice Department is using the criminal justice system to target and investigate him for politically vindictive reasons." They said the government had refused to offer assurances that it was preserving records and communications that would reveal the "motivations behind its investigations of Director Brennan."

"With this lawsuit, Director Brennan has served notice that the government's conduct and its document preservation will be carefully scrutinized in the event of any future indictment. Director Brennan will continue to vigorously defend himself against these baseless investigations, and he will challenge any attempt to use the criminal justice system for personal and political retribution," said Brennan's lawyers, Ken Wainstein and Dan Gelber.

As CIA director in the final years of President Barack Obama's Democratic administration, Brennan was a key figure in the U.S. intelligence community's conclusion that Russia had interfered in the 2016 presidential election on behalf of Trump, who went on to defeat Democrat Hillary Clinton for the White House. That assessment has for years infuriated Trump, who spent much of his first term shadowed by an investigation into whether his campaign had conspired with Russia.

Brennan over the last year has been entangled in Justice Department investigations into whether he made false statements before the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 and in a broader Florida-based inquiry into whether he and other former intelligence and law enforcement officials engaged in a conspiracy to keep Trump from power.

He has been subpoenaed to testify before a grand jury in the broader conspiracy investigation, though the date of his appearance has been postponed. His lawyers have said they've been told by prosecutors that he remains a target in the false statements investigation.

Brennan has vigorously denied any wrongdoing, with Wainstein telling Cobb during arguments last month that the notion of a broad anti-Trump conspiracy was "fiction."

It is unclear whether Brennan will face charges, but his attorneys sued in July to put the government on notice that they would challenge any prosecution on vindictive prosecution grounds. They said records they received from the government through a court order would help support their argument.

Cobb was nominated in 2021 by President Joe Biden, who earlier served as Obama's vice president.

articles.title: The White House won’t even try to explain Trump’s fictional inflation numbers
articles.summary: The actual inflation numbers aren’t good for President Donald Trump and his party. So Trump has come up with something of a solution: just use fake inflation...
articles.body:
The actual inflation numbers aren't good for President Donald Trump and his party. So Trump has come up with something of a solution: just use fake inflation numbers.

Trump has been lying about inflation throughout the midterm election campaign. Among other things, he has falsely declared he has "already stopped the inflation" (it accelerated again in September ), that "prices are now coming way down" (they have continued rising), and that prices are now "way down" from when former president Joe Biden left office in January 2025 (they are up 5.4% on average).

But in a series of rally speeches and comments to the press this week, Trump has gone a step further – deploying specific but phony numbers to make inflation seem better than it is.

In a Tuesday rally speech in Alaska, Trump claimed that there was just "1.7 inflation in the last three months. Think of that, 1.7. He (Biden) had real inflation; he had real inflation of 19%." On Wednesday, more than 12 hours after newly released Consumer Price Index figures showed a 3.7% year-over-year inflation rate in September, Trump repeated in a rally speech in Montana: "We inherited the worst inflation in history, think of it, and now, the last three months, we have 1.7 – we have it down to – he (Biden) had 19%, his real number's 19%."

Trump's figures are so bewildering that it is hard to figure out what exactly he is even talking about. The White House has so far ignored our requests for an explanation.

But we can think of three possible things Trump could conceivably be doing here and none of them would make his claims accurate. Heather Long, chief economist for Navy Federal Credit Union, said Thursday that "the 1.7% inflation figure is not supported by the data."

Possibility #1: Trump is simply lying about year-over-year inflation rates

For years , Trump has invented fictional economic numbers that work better for his purposes than the actual economic numbers. So it's very possible he's just lying about the year-over-year inflation rates that tend to be the most commonly discussed – wildly exaggerating the highest rate under Biden and significantly reducing the most recent rates this year.

In the last three months of 2026 for which Consumer Price Index (CPI) data is available, the year-over-year inflation rate was far higher than "1.7%": 3.7% in September , 3.4% in August and 3.4% in July . September data isn't yet available for the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, but that index shows the year-over-year rate was 3.4% in August, 3.4% in July and 3.5% in June .

This wouldn't be the first time he has made a false claim about having "1.7%" inflation for three months. In May, he falsely claimed that "just before the war" with Iran, "for the last three months, inflation was at 1.7%." That was wrong , too, and the White House could not offer any substantiation at the time.

Peak year-over-year inflation under Biden was 9.1%, in June 2022 , not "19%." So why do we suspect that Trump might be (incorrectly) referring to peak Biden-era inflation when he claims Biden was at "19%"? In a 2022 speech, Trump said Biden and Democrats had given the country 9.1% inflation, then quickly added, "It's not 9.1%. I believe it's double that."

It's not. The Consumer Price Index has its flaws and limitations , but there is no basis for any claim that the "real" figure is double the actual CPI figure.

Possibility #2: Trump is making a highly dishonest comparison of cumulative inflation

Cumulative inflation is the total increase in prices over a given period. There has been a 1.1% cumulative increase over the last three months, according to the CPI. That's not a "1.7%" increase, so cumulative inflation doesn't seem like what Trump is referring to, since he almost never uses a higher number when a lower number would be more helpful to him…

…but even if he was referring to cumulative inflation, his Trump-vs.-Biden comparison would be very deceptive. That's because there is no reasonable way to compare three-month inflation under Trump to "19%" inflation under Biden.

The total increase in prices over Biden's four-year term as president was 21.4% , according to the CPI, so "19%" is at least in the ballpark. But it would be completely nonsensical to contrast Biden-era cumulative inflation over 48 months with Trump-era cumulative inflation over three months.

Cumulative inflation during this Trump term to date, through 20 months, is 5.4% .

Possibility #3: Trump is misstating a fair point from his adviser

This wouldn't do anything to support Trump's "19%" figure for Biden. But it's possible that Trump's "1.7%" figure for the last three months is his inaccurate rendition of a fair point National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett made this week – "core" PCE inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was at an annualized rate of 2% for the three months from June through August.

This is the most generous reading of Trump's "1.7%" figure we can think of, but it would still mean Trump was not telling the truth. He didn't say in any of these comments that he was referring to core inflation rather than overall inflation; during an election in which gas prices are a major driver in overall inflation and a major factor in voter discontent, that's a big omission. And 2% is not "1.7%."

Also, the three-month PCE rate is widely expected to increase when the September figures for that index are released later in October. After the September CPI figures were released Wednesday, three-month core CPI jumped to an annualized rate of 3.4% – rising from the previous 2% after the September data replaced the June data in the calculation.

Long said the September data "changed the trend sharply. A key reason that 3-month annualized trend looked decent in August was due to falling gas prices in June and July." And she said that while a reference to core inflation is her "best guess" about where Trump got his number, "I still can't come up with 1.7%" without stripping out yet more price categories.

And one more thing: Biden didn't leave Trump the worst inflation ever

Trump has been saying at event after event that he inherited the worst inflation in US history from Biden. He didn't, as CNN and others have repeatedly noted.

The year-over-year inflation rate was 2.9% in Biden's last full month in office, December 2024, and 3% in January 2025, the month Trump took over partway through. Those numbers are unremarkable by historical standards, nowhere near any record, and lower than the rate every month since Trump launched a war with Iran early this year.

Trump could fairly say the 9.1% peak year-over-year inflation under Biden was the highest in more than 40 years. But even that 9.1% rate was much lower than the all-time high, 23.7% , or the highest point of Jimmy Carter's presidency, 14.8%, which was reached in 1980. And the rate then fell significantly before Trump returned to office.

The cumulative increase in prices from the beginning of Biden's administration to the end was also not the highest in US history; it was less than half of cumulative inflation during Carter's term.

CNN's Alicia Wallace contributed to this article.

articles.title: Ousted general warned of missile defense shortage before Iran war
articles.summary: Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George, later ousted by Defense Secretary Hegseth, said the shortage of missile defense munitions would extend into 2030.
articles.body:
Washington — In late December, two months before the U.S. war with Iran began, Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned that his service was critically short on missile defense munitions and that the shortage would last another five years, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ousted George in April, as the Iran war was underway.

George's risk analysis appeared in the Pentagon's Global Force Management Allocation Plan, a defense secretary-approved annual order determining where troops and weapons will be allocated across the globe, according to the U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News.

He warned that the stockpile of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense batteries and Patriot missiles would continue to be strategically low until 2030. His assessment was written for the Defense Department's plan for fiscal year 2027 and before the outbreak of the U.S.-Israel-led war with Iran, now in its seventh month.

U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly said his assessment stemmed from the transfer of Patriots to Ukraine after Russia's invasion in 2022, the expenditure of munitions to defend Israel, and the reduced capacity of the defense industrial base.

CBS News is withholding the exact percentage figures conveyed by U.S. officials because of security concerns, and George declined to comment. U.S. officials say that while the U.S. possesses a significant stockpile of some offensive munitions, like the Joint Direct Attack Munition and Small Diameter Bombs, missile defense munitions used in Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, batteries, and Patriot missile systems are at low strategic-risk levels.

The THAAD system is one of the U.S. military's most advanced missile defense systems, designed to intercept and destroy incoming ballistic missiles during the final phase of their flight, either inside or just outside Earth's atmosphere. The Army has eight THAAD batteries. Each battery consists of 90 soldiers who operate six truck-mounted launchers, with each truck possessing eight launchers. A full battery controls 48 interceptors, according to a 2025 report from the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service.

The Patriot air-defense system is designed to protect military installations, troops and other critical infrastructure from incoming ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as hostile aircraft. It can engage a broader range of aerial threats at lower altitudes than a THAAD battery, but when used together, they provide even more effective overlapping layers of defense against missile attacks.

The Patriot munition at a critical low is the Patriot Advanced Capability-3, or PAC-3, a high-velocity surface-to-air interceptor designed to destroy incoming tactical ballistic missiles and cruise missiles by ramming into them. PAC-3s can also bring down enemy aircraft, according to U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News.

"Those are the two Army munitions that would be most heavily used in a conflict with China," said Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and CSIS Defense and Security senior adviser. "You're not gonna use that many Javelins, for example, because the amount of ground combat is going to be relatively limited, even artillery will be limited, but air defense — missile defense — that will be huge."

An April estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies showed that it currently takes defense contractors four years and five months to complete delivery of new THAAD interceptor contracts. Patriot PAC-3 interceptor orders have an average delivery time of three and a half years.

CSIS' estimate said that before the Iran war, the U.S. entered 2026 with roughly 2,300 or so Patriot interceptors and expended between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict, potentially consuming as much as 61% of its prewar inventory. Fewer than 500 replenishment munitions were expected to be delivered in fiscal year 2026.

The stockpile for THAAD systems prior to the Iran war sat at around 355 interceptors, with the Iran war using between 190 to 290, or about 82% of its prewar inventory, according to CSIS. There were no expected deliveries for replenishment in fiscal year 2026. In the current fiscal year — 2027 — the U.S. has requested more than 800 THAADs.

Two of the nation's largest defense contractors — Lockheed Martin and RTX, through its Raytheon business — are involved in manufacturing these systems and their key components. They've recently signed agreements aimed at accelerating production.

In January, Lockheed Martin announced a plan to quadruple the production capacity of THAADs from 96 to 400 interceptors per year.

While the war with Iran has caused missile defense munitions to be depleted at a much higher rate, decades of Pentagon spending decisions, a shrinking defense industrial base and successive military operations that consume weapons faster than manufacturers can replace them have contributed to the current shortages.

One U.S. official told CBS News that even if the United States could avoid expending additional THAAD or Patriot munitions in Iran or in other conflicts, it would take until the midterm elections of the next presidential administration — 2030 — to replenish the stockpile to the already-low December 2025 levels.

Contacted by CBS News, Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell said, "Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false. When the Fake News media irresponsibly amplifies these lies, the real-world consequences is clear: our enemies are emboldened to provide — or attack — American troops."

He added that the U.S. still has "everything required to strike at the time and place of the President's choosing."

"Across multiple combatant commands," Parnell said, "we have already executed successful operations while maintaining a deep, ready arsenal to defend our people and our interests."

The U.S. military is divided into 11 unified combatant commands, each responsible for either a region of the world or specialized military mission. For operations against Iran, U.S. Central Command, led by Navy Adm. Brad Cooper, is in charge.

Each combatant command needs a certain number of troops and weapons. The Pentagon uses a framework known as Global Force Management to decide where American troops, their units and some of the military's most sought-after weapons are sent around the world.

The Global Force Management Allocation Plan, or GFMAP, is at the center of the process, laying out which forces will be provided to combatant commanders, for what missions and for how long.

The plan is typically organized around the federal fiscal year. Generally, the Pentagon enters a new fiscal year with an existing plan for many of the forces expected to deploy or remain deployed during the coming 12 to 24 months, rather than deciding from scratch each time a commander asks for troops or weapons.

But the plan is not set in stone. Wars erupt, crises develop, missions end and commanders are faced with unanticipated events to address.

For instance, the commander of U.S. European Command might want more Patriots in Poland at the same time that U.S. Central Command wants those same resources in Kuwait, while U.S. Indo-Pacific Command may also need the systems for contingencies involving China.

There's a constant shuffling of troops and assets from one region to another — in one instance in April 2025, Adm. Samuel Paparo, the commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, told the Senate Armed Services Committee that the Army had transferred a Patriot battalion from his region to U.S. Central Command amid ongoing fighting with the Iranian-back Houthi rebels in Yemen.

What led to the current weapons systems shortage?

After the collapse of the Soviet Union, American military planners abandoned the assumption that the U.S. might need to fight a prolonged war against another superpower, explained Cancian.

"After the Cold War, we planned on fighting short regional conflicts against countries like Iraq or North Korea. And for those countries we didn't need the large inventories that we had needed during the Cold War," Cancian said. "We needed much smaller inventories."

He added: "We shrank the industrial base. There was the famous 'Last Supper' which was literally a dinner that the deputy defense secretary put on for the heads of the defense industry, and he told them there's not enough money to keep you all in business, so you're going to have to consolidate or move out of the business, which they did."

The resulting mergers reduced the number of major aerospace and defense contractors from 51 to five, according to the CSIS analysis.

Also, historically, the Pentagon's procurement decisions have reduced spending on ammunition and missiles to free up money for fighter jets, tanks and warships, even while acknowledging that those weapons are essential to war fighting.

Cancian told CBS News that the consolidation of the defense industrial base shaped an industry that produces efficiently during peacetime but is not designed to surge production.

"We squeezed all the surge out because it was seen as unnecessary. So, that's where we end up when the war in Ukraine begins," said Cancian. "And after six months or so, we realized that we just don't have enough munitions and equipment for a protracted conflict."

Under the Biden administration, there was a renewed interest in building surge capabilities back into the defense industrial base but that would take time. As the war between Russia and Ukraine began in full, the U.S. transferred roughly 600 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine. However, not all of those weapons came from American military stockpiles; some were manufactured through the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative or provided by European countries.

Additionally, both Biden and Trump administrations used Patriot and THAAD missile interceptors to defend Israel against Iranian strikes. Six months before Gen. George's warning assessment, U.S. forces fired roughly 150 THAAD interceptors and almost 80 Patriot interceptors during the Twelve Day War.

Cancian noted that the five-year timeline to bring Patriot and THAAD stockpiles just to the low pre-Iran war levels is based on the assumption that the production schedule stays on track — and that additional military operations do not further deplete the inventory.

articles.title: Hasan Piker rips New York Jewish voters' shift away from Democrats, blames Israel
articles.summary: Hasan Piker faced antisemitism accusations after claiming Jewish voters are leaving the Democratic Party solely over Israel foreign policy.
articles.body:
Jewish voters in New York appear to be moving away from the Democratic Party, and controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker blamed the shift on their support for Israel.

On Wednesday, Piker responded to a CNN clip in which the network's chief data analyst, Harry Enten, and anchor John Berman discussed the drop in support for Democrats among Jewish voters, expressing dismay that they were shifting away from the party.

"It's wild that this many jewish voters are leaving the democratic party over israel. It's not like the republican alternatives are presenting a more appealing policy agenda, it's just israel! It's literally over the continuation of israel's belligerence. A real shame," Piker wrote on X .

In the segment, Enten explained that Jewish support for New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, dropped since her last election in 2022, according to recent Siena Polling . Enten then revealed that Democrats' advantage over Republicans among Jewish voters in New York had narrowed by 36 points since 2022, according to Siena Polling averages.

"State of New York U.S. House polling among Jewish voters. Look at this. In 2018, Democrats were ahead by 40 points," Enten said. "In 2022, 49 points. Look at this, the average of polls this year. Its just 13 points. It's just 13 points. That is a shift of, what, 36 points, 36 points away from the Democrats. Their lead has absolutely tumbled into the Hudson River among Jewish voters.

"Yes, they are still ahead. But we are talking about historically strong numbers for Republicans among Jewish voters," the analyst added.

"It definitely seems to me that the developments over the past few years, at least in New York, at least in this polling, (have) had a huge impact on how Jewish voters say they are going to vote, not just for governor, but for Congress as well."

Piker faced backlash over his assertion that the shift was solely about Israel, with Republican Jewish Coalition communications director Sam Markstein telling Fox News Digital that the streamer's accusation was rooted in an antisemitic trope.

"Hasan Piker's statement that American Jews' voting preferences are all about Middle East policy plays directly into the oldest antisemitic trope of dual loyalty. He is flat out wrong and is trivializing the very real spike in Jew hatred which directly threatens our community's safety," Markstein said.

"Let's be clear: American Jews are fleeing the Democratic Party because its leadership continues to elevate, embrace and appease the most radicalized elements of their anti-America extremist party base. The sad irony is that antisemitic bigot Hasan Piker, who said 'America deserved 9/11,' and who has been elevated by national Democrats, including campaigning with Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, is Exhibit A," he added.

Shai Davidai, a former Columbia University professor and author of "American Intellectual Antisemitism," also responded to Piker on X , saying, "It's not 'over Israel.' It's over people like you."

New York Post columnist Karol Markowicz argued in her response to Piker that Jewish voters have reasons to shift away from Democrats that go beyond Israel.

"Even setting aside support for Israel, which Jews should absolutely not, Jews are regularly assaulted in NY and no Democrats care. They aren't allowed to defend themselves and the mayor regularly riles up the attackers. Easy call to vote Republican," Markowicz wrote on X .

Piker, who has long been a vocal critic of Israel, has criticized Jewish Americans' support for the Jewish state. In August, the streamer was panned by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle after he said, "People don't f--- with Israel any longer. And if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they're singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone will come around and take action not against Israel, mind you, but against American Jews."

Critics accused Piker of blaming Jews for antisemitic attacks against them. Democratic Sens. Elissa Slotkin , D-Mich., and Jacky Rosen, D-Nev., condemned Piker's remarks.

"This shouldn't be hard: no community should face the threat [of] violence for their political views. Period," Slotkin wrote in a statement posted to social media . "That goes if you're pro-Israel, pro-Palestine, pro-choice, pro-life or any other cause you care about. And blaming the victims of violence for bringing it on themselves only further endangers people."

Rosen said the remarks were "a new low" for the controversial Twitch streamer.

"Blaming Jewish Americans for the violence and hate they're facing is not just wrong, it provides an excuse to those perpetuating these anti-Jewish hate crimes," Rosen said in a statement .

"Let me be absolutely clear: crimes against Jews for being Jews is antisemitism plain and simple. There's no excuse for it."

Other Democrats joined in condemning Piker, including Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J.; House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.; and Reps. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J.; Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y.; Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla.; Brad Schneider, D-Ill.; Greg Stanton, D-Ariz.; and Hillary Scholten, D-Mich.

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who was criticized for campaigning with Piker, distanced himself from the streamer after the controversial remarks.

"I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past," El-Sayed wrote on X .

"My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters," he added. "Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk."

Fox News Digital reached out to Hasan Piker for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Republican Jewish Coalition communications director Sam Markstein told Fox News Digital that Piker's remarks reflect an antisemitic trope.

articles.title: Trump invokes executive privilege in Kennedy Center court fight
articles.summary: A White House lawyer said information about the president’s management of the center, including efforts to add his name to it, should be off-limits.
articles.body: A White House lawyer said President Donald Trump has officially invoked executive privilege in the court fight involving his management of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. In a court filing late Wednesday, Joshua Hoyt, a deputy assistant and deputy counsel to the president, said that at “the direction of the President,” he was “formally invoking the presidential communications privilege with respect to information, documents, and communications requested” by the plaintiff in the case, Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio. Beatty, an ex officio board member of the center, has been challenging Trump’s efforts to add his name to the front of the building and his directive that the center be shuttered for two years while it’s renovated. She’s been seeking more information about Trump’s role in both matters, since he named himself to the board last year and was voted chairman by his handpicked board members. In February, Trump directed the center to be closed for renovations in a social media post and has since said those renovations won’t proceed if he doesn’t get “recognition” for his efforts. Beatty contends the board’s subsequent votes to close the center were a fait accompli, given Trump’s February directive. In the administration’s court filing Wednesday, Hoyt said the executive privilege invocation means Beatty is not entitled to any more details about the president’s management of the nonprofit board. He said in a declaration that privilege specifically covers “information, documents, and communications shared between the President, his advisors (government and non-government), and Kennedy Center staff, pertaining to the management and operation” of the center. It also extends to communications “to or from his advisors and/or Kennedy Center staff.” In a separate filing Wednesday, the Justice Department said Beatty was engaged in an improper “fishing expedition,” arguing her “pursuit of irrelevant evidence does not justify her extraordinary request” for additional documents and information. Beatty’s attorneys asserted it was the DOJ that was acting in extraordinary fashion. “Donald Trump appointed himself as chair of the non-profit board of the Kennedy Center, and is now trying to shield his management by improperly invoking executive privilege,” the lawyers, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group, said in a statement. “The Supreme Court has stressed that the government should not invoke executive privilege lightly, but that is precisely what the Department of Justice is doing here. This kind of cover-up is a direct assault on the rule of law,” they said. Lawyers for the DOJ had said in a filing earlier this month that Trump would be claiming executive privilege, but he did not formally do so until Wednesday. In an Oct. 6 filing, Beatty’s attorneys said there were no grounds to claim the privilege, since Trump is a defendant in the case as chairman of the congressionally created center’s board, and not as president. The attorneys said the Kennedy Center is not part of the executive branch “and does not exercise executive power.” They added that Trump “voluntarily assumed the ‘usual powers and obligations of a trustee.’” “Trustee and board chair are not roles that must be performed by the President of the United States and, indeed, never have been in the Center’s history before now. Nor are the staff at the Kennedy Center anything like the close presidential advisers whose conversations executive privilege protects,” the lawyers argued. “The Court should not permit Defendants to evade accountability as trustees by abusing a privilege constructed for other purposes, not the chairmanship of this non-profit entity.” “Allowing Defendants to hide behind this unwarranted assertion of privilege would obstruct the search for the truth” and “undermine public confidence in these important proceedings,” they added. The Justice Department countered that Trump’s involvement with the center “is undoubtedly in his official capacity,” since it’s the president’s duty to appoint board members. And, the government lawyers said, the president is always the president. Beatty “argues that executive privilege ‘protects the institution of the Presidency, not the individual who happens to occupy the White House.’ But, as the Supreme Court reinforced recently, the Framers vested ‘the executive Power’ in one person—‘a President of the United States of America.’” The federal judge presiding over the case, Christopher Cooper, has not yet weighed in on the issue, but the administration’s stance conflicts with a ruling he issued this month allowing Beatty’s team to learn more about the circumstances surrounding a photo of Trump on Air Force One viewing a poster that read “Kennedy Center DEMOLISH.” The venue was closed Sept. 15 on a temporary basis for what center officials described as emergency safety assessments. It has not reopened.

articles.title: Trump lashes out at Republicans as Ken Paxton struggles in Texas
articles.summary: The president singled out Karl Rove and incumbent Sen. John Cornyn as his endorsed candidate appears to be in a tight race with James Talarico.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump is blaming fellow Republicans as his endorsed candidate, Ken Paxton, appears to be in a fierce struggle for a Senate seat in Texas with Democratic challenger James Talarico in a state the GOP has long taken for granted.

Trump, in a lengthy post to Truth Social Thursday, singled out longtime Republican strategist Karl Rove and Sen. John Cornyn, the incumbent who failed to secure the president's endorsement in a heated primary.

Rove and Cornyn, Trump said, are doing "everything possible" to make it harder for Paxton to defeat Talarico, a state lawmaker and Presbyterian seminarian who is making a suprisingly strong run for Senate in deep red Texas.

"They are hurting Texas and, more importantly, hurting the United States of America!" Trump wrote. "If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career."

Cornyn, a longtime fixture in Texas politics, lost his bid for reelection in a contentious Republican primary in which he and his supporters portrayed Paxton as a deeply flawed candidate. As Election Day approaches, public polling over the past two months has shown Talarico with a narrow edge against Paxton, the state's attorney general.

Trump urged his supporters to back Paxton.

"Your favorite President (ME!) is asking all of those who supported Senator John Cornyn to UNITE, and immediately switch your support to Ken Paxton," Trump said. "He will be a Great Senator, just like he is a Great Attorney General. "

The race has also become one of the most expensive non-presidential battles. Talarico raised $64 million this summer — the largest third-quarter haul of any Senate candidate in history. He has raised more than $134 million since launching his campaign last year.

Paxton raised $18 million in the third quarter of 2026 and last month announced a new $20 million ad buy . Earlier this month, though, a Trump operative told POLITICO that MAGA Inc. and its affiliates are could spend nearly $45 million on direct mail, TV and digital advertising in Texas through Oct. 12.

Already, $235 million has been spent by outside conservative groups and party committees against Talarico as national Republicans scramble to boost Paxton.

Some Republicans have grown concerned that the cost of the Texas race is diverting money needed in other states and have expressed frustrations with Paxton after leaked audio showed him blaming Trump for his woes.

Trump easily won Texas in 2024 , winning just over 56% of the vote. But concerns about Republicans' chances this November have surged as the president's approval rating plummets.

articles.title: Datafolha e Quaest: Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula têm empate técnico | G1
articles.standfirst: Datafolha aponta Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) com 47% e Lula (PT) com 45%; na Quaest, o senador tem 46%, contra 44% do presidente. A diferença entre os candidatos está dentro da margem de erro nos dois levantamentos.
articles.summary: A pesquisa presidencial 2026 do Datafolha e Quaest aponta Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula com diferença de dois pontos, configurando empate técnico no segundo turno.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula — Foto: REUTERS/Diego Vara e REUTERS/Adriano Machado

As duas pesquisas presidenciais mais recentes, divulgadas pelo Datafolha e pela Quaest, mostram um cenário de empate técnico entre Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e o presidente Lula (PT) na disputa pelo segundo turno das eleições de 2026. Nos dois levantamentos, a diferença está dentro da margem de erro.

Na pesquisa Datafolha, divulgada nesta quinta-feira (15), Flávio Bolsonaro tem 47% das intenções de voto, contra 45% de Lula. Já o levantamento da Quaest, divulgado na quarta-feira (14), aponta o candidato do PL com 46% e o presidente com 44%.

As duas pesquisas têm margem de erro de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e nível de confiança de 95%.

Datafolha, 2º turno: estimulada — Foto: Arte/g1

Quaest, 2º turno: intenção de voto para presidente — Foto: Arte/g1

Datafolha aponta oscilação na vantagem de Flávio Bolsonaro

O levantamento do Datafolha mostra que a diferença entre os dois candidatos oscilou em relação à semana passada.

Flávio Bolsonaro passou de 49% para 47% das intenções de voto, uma oscilação negativa de dois pontos percentuais. Lula, por sua vez, manteve os mesmos 45% registrados na pesquisa anterior.

Com isso, a vantagem numérica do candidato do PL caiu de quatro para dois pontos percentuais.

O percentual de eleitores que declararam voto branco, nulo ou em nenhum dos candidatos passou de 5% para 6%. Já a parcela de indecisos aumentou de 1% para 2%.

Quaest também registra diferença de dois pontos

A primeira pesquisa Quaest realizada para o segundo turno apresenta um cenário semelhante ao identificado pelo Datafolha.

No levantamento, Flávio Bolsonaro aparece com 46% das intenções de voto, enquanto Lula registra 44%. Outros 9% afirmam que pretendem votar em branco, anular o voto ou não comparecer às urnas, e 1% está indeciso.

Embora os percentuais sejam ligeiramente diferentes dos registrados pelo Datafolha, as duas pesquisas apontam a mesma distância numérica entre os candidatos: dois pontos percentuais.

O Datafolha entrevistou 2.520 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais entre os dias 13 e 14 de outubro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, com nível de confiança de 95%. O levantamento está registrado na Justiça Eleitoral sob o número BR-00466/2026.

A Quaest ouviu 2.154 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais entre os dias 10 e 13 de outubro. A margem de erro também é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, com nível de confiança de 95%. O registro na Justiça Eleitoral é BR-08729/2026.

articles.title: Primeira Turma do STF começa a julgar  nesta sexta denúncia e pode tornar réu blogueiro aliado de Bolsonaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Oswaldo Eustáquio é acusado de associação criminosa por postagens e participação em manifestações contra diplomação e posse de Lula. Defesa fala em julgamento à revelia.
articles.summary: Oswaldo Eustáquio é acusado de associação criminosa por postagens e participação em manifestações contra diplomação e posse de Lula. Defesa fala em julgamento à revelia.
articles.body:
A Primeira Turma do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) deve começar a julgar nesta sexta-feira (16) se torna réu o blogueiro Oswaldo Eustáquio, apoiador do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro.

De acordo com a PGR, a conduta ficou configurada por postagens nas redes sociais e pela participação em manifestações contra a diplomação e posse do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT).

O caso tramita em segredo de justiça no STF. Os votos dos ministros podem ser inseridos no sistema eletrônico da Corte até o dia 23 de outubro.

Na denúncia, a PGR apontou que Eustáquio também participou de mobilizações em frente a unidades militares, associou-se a centenas de outras pessoas, com o objetivo de praticar atos que se voltavam contra a legitimidade do sistema eleitoral e contra o Estado Democrático de Direito.

A defesa de Oswaldo Eustáquio tem afirmado que o julgamento será à revelia e sem seguir o devido processo legal. Em uma rede social, Oswaldo Eustáquio afirmou nesta quinta-feira (15) que o julgamento à revelia é um "absurdo".

"O Alexandre de Moraes não nomeou um advogado dativo, um defensor público, para ver o meu caso. Eles vão me julgar à revelia, pelo crime de ter cantado se precisar, a gente acampa, ou o ladrão não sobe a rampa, por associação criminosa, sem dizer com quem que eu me associei criminalmente".

Em agosto, Moraes determinou a notificação de Eustáquio por edital, abrindo prazo para resposta à acusação.

O blogueiro bolsonarista Oswaldo Eustáquio, investigado por atos antidemocráticos — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Eustáquio participou publicamente dos acampamentos que pediam um golpe de Estado e, segundo a Polícia Federal (PF), chegou a se refugiar no Palácio da Alvorada com medo de ser preso no fim de 2022.

Em setembro, Moraes arquivou uma investigação contra Oswaldo Eustáquio, o senador Marcos do Val (Avante-ES), Allan dos Santos, e Ednardo D’Ávila Mello Raposo por suspeitas de obstrução de investigações e incitação ao crime, seguindo entendimento da PGR.

O blogueiro chegou a ser preso no Brasil, foi colocado em prisão domiciliar e fugiu para a Espanha em 2023. Ele é alvo de dois mandados de prisão preventiva por crimes contra a democracia, obstrução de justiça, divulgação de dados protegidos, perseguição, ameaça e corrupção de menores.

Em dezembro de 2025, a Justiça da Espanha rejeitou recurso do governo brasileiro e negou a extradição do blogueiro Oswaldo Eustáquio em razão do critério de "dupla incidência criminal" e por entender que há "motivação política" na investigação.

O acordo entre os países exige que a conduta criminosa atribuída ao extraditado seja prevista na lei penal do Brasil e da Espanha – ou seja, um crime tipificado nos dois países. A Espanha veda extradição em casos de “crimes políticos ou conexos a este”.

State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in an interview Thursday evening with NewsNation’s Kellie Meyer that the ousted secretary’s time had come to…
articles.body:
Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem is no longer serving as the Trump administration’s special envoy to the “ Shield of the Americas ” coalition, a spokesperson confirmed to NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcasting partner.

State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in an interview Thursday evening with NewsNation’s Kellie Meyer that the ousted secretary’s time had come to an end as special envoy, though he did not elaborate on the reasoning behind her departure.

“We’ve seen the secretary’s time as envoy expire,” Pigott said. “She continues to be at the State Department as a senior adviser.”

CBS News was the first to report Noem was no longer in her role.

President Trump announced Noem would assume the role of special envoy for the newly created Shield of the Americas initiative after she was fired as Homeland Security secretary in March. Her removal from the department’s highest office followed controversial immigration enforcement operations, leading to the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis — one of whom Noem branded a “ domestic terrorist .”

Noem’s Homeland Security tenure was shrouded in controversy, including scrutiny surrounding her relationship and association with Corey Lewandowski, a former adviser for the department. House Democrats opened an investigation into Lewandowski in March.

Pigott said Thursday that Noem would remain working on the Shield of the Americas initiative but declined to provide specifics on what this would entail.

“There’s always these types of changes that happen,” Pigott said. “This is part of what’s happening with these positions. But, certainly, we remain dedicated to implementing the president’s agenda across the board.”

articles.title: Collins, Jackson trade jabs in final Maine Senate debate: 3 takeaways
articles.summary: Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) faced off against Democratic candidate Troy Jackson on Thursday in the final Senate debate before Maine voters head to the polls. The two traded jabs over President Trump, campaign financing, immigration reform and their voting record as the Senate race enters its final stretch. Collins stressed her bipartisan approach to voting…
articles.body:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) faced off against Democratic candidate Troy Jackson on Thursday in the final Senate debate before Maine voters head to the polls.

The two traded jabs over President Trump, campaign financing, immigration reform and their voting record as the Senate race enters its final stretch.

Collins stressed her bipartisan approach to voting and did not blindly follow her party or Trump, while Jackson, a former state Senate president, repeatedly looked to tie her to Trump’s agenda.

The hour-long debate, hosted by Maine Public in collaboration with The Portland Herald, heated up as the two levied accusations at one another.

At one point, a protester off camera interrupted the debate, and could be heard shouting at Collins, “AI data centers are destroying our climate.”

“This is obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” Collins said, which Jackson quickly denied.

The closely watched race has Collins, a five-term incumbent, fighting to hold onto her seat in blue-leaning Maine, against Jackson, who became the party’s nominee after Graham Platner dropped out due to sexual assault allegations and a texting scandal.

Here are three takeaways from Thursday night’s debate:

Collins pressed to prove independence from Trump

Collins looked to distance herself from Trump and other members of his administration but faced questions about whether her opposition to the president has actually changed the outcome of major votes in Washington, D.C.

When asked to name a time where she voted against Trump and significantly changed the outcome, Collins pointed to her efforts to block Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s confirmation.

Collins said she had organized Republican opposition to his nomination, but another GOP senator changed his mind at the last minute. She was quickly called out for not changing the outcome of a vote, with Hegseth still leading the Pentagon.

The Maine Republican acknowledged that while her effort ultimately fell short, an analysis had found 56 instances in which her votes changed an outcome. Collins did not specify which votes she was referencing.

Jackson pounced on the moment and accused Collins of only breaking with Trump and the GOP when her vote is not needed.

“The reality is that 100 percent of the time, when Donald Trump needs her, Susan Collins is going to be there,” Jackson said.

The Democrat pointed to Collins’s vote to advance Trump’s sweeping tax and spending bill, despite her eventual opposition to the final legislation.

Collins pushed back, arguing that a broader review of her record showed she sided with the president 72 percent of the time, rather than 90 to 100 percent as claimed.

She also touted her record of voting to confirm three liberal Supreme Court justices — Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Kentanji Brown Jackson — who were nominated by different Democratic presidents in the past.

Collins turned the tables on Jackson during a fiery exchange over campaign financing, accusing the Democrat of breaking his promise to reject money from billionaires and corporate political action committees.

Jackson admitted Thursday that his Senate campaign received donations from billionaires despite the promise, receiving a noticeable reaction from the audience.

“As far as the billionaires that I might have on my campaign, that is accurate,” Jackson said, before insisting that the contributions would not influence his votes.

“I’m going to tax those billionaires when I get to the U.S. Senate,” he continued. “So, if they want to give me money during this campaign, I guess that’s up to them.”

He acknowledged receiving $15,000 from the oil and pharmaceutical industry, saying he had donated the money to charities in keeping up with his campaign pledge.

Collins also criticized Jackson for missing his self-imposed deadline to release his campaign finance report by one day, which he said was delayed because of the flurry of contributions his campaign had received.

The Iran war emerged as a major point of contention in the debate, with Jackson arguing that Collins had failed to use her powerful position as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee to help put an end to the conflict.

“The way to block it now would be to shut off funding,” he said.

Collins has repeatedly criticized Trump’s handling of the war and pointed to numerous votes she cast against continuing military operations.

Jackson also pointed to the conflict’s effects on the economy, including rising fuel prices that have hit Maine’s fishing and logging industries particularly hard.

Collins argued that Congress should have had a say in the decision to go to war.

“Congress definitely should have been consulted,” she said, defending her votes to halt the conflict after the initial 60-day period under the War Powers Act.

articles.title: Trump looms as tensions flare in final Maine Senate debate
articles.summary: The marathon of debates in the Maine Senate race has ended, but there is still one unanswered question: Just how large will President Donald Trump loom in November?
articles.body: BANGOR, Maine — The marathon of debates in the Maine Senate race has ended, but there is still one unanswered question: Just how large will President Donald Trump loom in November? That question was at the center of the clashes between Democrat Troy Jackson and longtime GOP Sen. Susan Collins as they faced off in four debates over the last two weeks, including a finale Thursday hosted by Maine Public Broadcasting Network, the Portland Press Herald and NBC affiliate WCSH of Portland. Jackson is betting voters’ views of Trump, who has never won Maine, will dominate their views of this Senate race, which could determine which party controls the chamber next year. He repeatedly tied Collins to Trump throughout all four debates. Collins, meanwhile, tried to appeal to Mainers who want a senator willing to break with his or her party. “I voted against my own party more often than any other senator on either side of the aisle,” Collins said during the final debate. “That is not something that Troy could ever say. He’s going to be an automatic vote for the Democratic position, no matter what. We have lost a lot of the centrists, and one reason I’m running again is we need people who will work across party lines.” Jackson countered: “The reality is that 100% of the time, when Donald Trump needs her, Susan Collins is going to be there. That has happened time and time again.” Trump’s policies were intertwined with the major topics covered in all four debates, including high costs, the war in Iran, immigration enforcement and an ongoing trade war with Canada, which Maine borders. On Thursday, Collins was also pressed about her support for some Trump Cabinet officials, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. She said she didn’t regret having voted to confirm him while noting that she disagrees with Kennedy’s vaccine skepticism. Collins said Kennedy has helped release more funds from a program to help low-income Mainers buy heating oil amid soaring prices. Jackson, meanwhile, said he would vote to convict Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on impeachment charges. “But that’s not my focus,” he quickly added. “My focus is delivering healthcare, prescription drugs, child care, the things that Mainers need right now more than ever, and getting out of the Iran war so we can stabilize prices.” Tensions were high after four debates in rapid succession. This one was the first in front of a live audience, with roughly 200 people gathered in a theater at Husson University. Around 20 minutes into the debate, a young man stood and shouted about his concerns about data centers, exclaiming that he was scared for the future. “Thirty years for what?” the protester shouted as he was escorted out of the theater, referring to Collins’ time in the Senate. Collins claimed the protester was a Jackson supporter, and Jackson remarked, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.” While the protester questioned her decades in the Senate, Collins has argued that her seniority makes her an effective advocate for Maine. She often touts her role as chairwoman of the powerful Appropriations Committee, arguing she has helped bring home huge sums of federal money to fund projects in the state. Collins stressed that she has broken with Trump on some key issues, noting she voted against Trump’s sweeping “big, beautiful” tax and spending law last year, though she did vote to allow the measure to proceed on the floor. “I nevertheless voted against the bill, even though it was the president’s top legislative priority. I’ve also voted nine times against the president on the Iran war,” she said. Jackson has argued that Collins could have done more to oppose the military action. Asked where he would break with his own party, Jackson pointed to his pledge not to accept donations from corporate political action committees. “I think the Democrats are still too close to that,” Jackson said. “I don’t accept corporate PACs. I don’t accept corporate money. This is a campaign about fighting for everyday working-class people, and that’s one thing that I’ve been consistent on.” Collins tried to undermine that argument, using her one question to ask Jackson about ads run in coordination with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which does accept corporate PAC money. Jackson countered that he doesn’t approve those ads. While he acknowledged he has had some support from billionaires, he said his campaign is powered by small-dollar donors. Jackson raised more than $20 million from July through September, according to a fundraising report filed Thursday. That is nearly four times Collins’ $5.2 million haul over the same period. Jackson, a former state Senate president and logger, then pressed Collins about her claims that he couldn’t be effective in the Senate. “I have the experience fighting for working-class people, and they deserve a senator that respects them. Is it just me that you look down on, or is it working-class people overall?” he asked. “Troy, I do not look down on you or on anyone. I grew up in Caribou. My first job was picking potatoes,” Collins countered, saying she has “literally” worked since she was 10 years old. “I have supported all the social safety net programs,” she said later. Collins’ experience in the Senate is a major reason her supporters are backing her for a sixth term. “He is just not strong on the mechanics of government,” Collins supporter Mary Ann Lynch said of Jackson. Lynch is a lifelong Democrat but is backing Collins. And she said in a phone interview Wednesday that the debates hadn’t changed her mind. “Just watching the debates, it’s hard for me to say that if we sent Troy Jackson to Washington, he would ever be able to cut a path of leadership,” said Lynch, 71, a former member of the Cape Elizabeth Town Council. But Jackson’s push to tie Collins to Trump does resonate with voters leaning toward supporting him, like Dan Tremble. Tremble, a Penobscot County commissioner, said he was “pretty solid” in his decision to support Jackson as he entered the theater in Bangor on Thursday night. “Susan Collins has done a lot for the state of Maine,” Tremble, 61, a Democrat, said when he was asked why he wasn’t certain he’d support Jackson. “But I think having her in the Senate, I think, would still leave a majority for the president in the United States Senate, and that’s very worrisome with this president.” “He says, ‘Vote like I’m on the ballot,’” Tremble added, referring to Trump. “I will.” CORRECTION (Oct. 15, 2026, 10:17 p.m. ET): A previous version of this article misidentified the Cabinet secretary Troy Jackson said he’d vote to convict on impeachment charges. It was Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, not Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

articles.title: Argentine students protest on campus over Milei’s austerity
articles.summary: Judge fines the government for failing to fund universities as protests over Milei’s cuts turn violent.
articles.body:
“This cannot go on!” students shout during an assembly in the middle of the central hall of the University of Buenos Aires Exact and Natural Sciences building.

It is part of Argentina’s prestigious public university system.

The faculty’s central hall is covered with dozens of banners protesting President Javier Milei’s spending cuts. Students have called an assembly to announce the occupation of the university, a traditional form of protest in Argentina meant to raise public awareness and pressure the government.

They say they will take over the building for a day. Many students and professors here are concerned about the impact of Milei’s austerity policies on public universities and say the future of free higher education is at risk.

“Our best professors are leaving en masse. With salaries that cannot cover their basic needs, they are leaving for private universities,” Emiliano Gato, a physics student who is part of the group, told Al Jazeera.

“I dream of doing research and teaching at the public University of Buenos Aires. It’s a prestigious school. But now, with this austerity plan, I don’t know what will happen.”

Public universities in Argentina have become a major battleground of Milei’s austerity plan. Students and professors are protesting the lack of funding and the erosion of salaries, which they say is a major threat to the country’s public education.

Milei is implementing one of the harshest austerity plans in Argentina’s history.

Since taking office in 2023, he has laid off thousands of state employees, shut down ministries, reduced subsidies and cut government-funded programmes. The measures were meant to fight high inflation, which was a major problem in Argentina. Almost three years later, inflation has fallen to around 2 percent a month. Milei says his plan is going well.

“Argentina is growing at a remarkable pace. We have now recorded 27 consecutive months of sustained growth, and today the country is expanding at four times its historical rate. This growth is being felt across almost every sector of the economy,” said Milei during a recent visit to Washington.

But not everyone agrees. His plan is also having a profound impact on public education, welfare plans for people with disabilities, pensioners and others who depend on state support. The opposition has tried to block many of Milei’s reforms.

Last year, Congress overturned presidential vetoes and approved two laws, one increasing funding for public universities and another declaring a disability emergency. But Milei’s government has refused to implement them, arguing that Congress failed to identify how they would be financed.

A federal judge has now begun fining the government 100,000 pesos (around $70) a day for failing to implement parts of the financing law, which requires Milei’s government to restore university salaries and student scholarships lost to inflation, regularly update budgets and provide funding for research, hospitals and infrastructure.

And that’s why thousands of people took to the streets on Thursday to demand that the government implement it. All around Buenos Aires, long columns of people blocked the centre of the city as they called for a general strike. Although the protest was meant to be peaceful, it soon turned violent. Police fired tear gas and rubber bullets as protesters threw rocks.

The plaza in front of Congress resembled a battleground. At least 25 people were detained, and several others were injured, including members of the security forces.

Maria Teresa de Jesus is a professor in the University of Buenos Aires chemistry department. She says she makes around $700 a month and it has become difficult to make ends meet. “I have come to this protest as a last resort. I am professor. I love teaching, doing research. I shouldn’t be here,” she told Al Jazeera. “Public education is crucial in this country, to make education accessible to all. And the government is ignoring it.”

Many in Argentina continue to support Milei’s economic plan. They are hoping the government’s plan to exploit the country’s vast natural resources will pay off and translate into more jobs, higher wages and improved living standards.

But many others have stopped believing and are prepared to raise the stakes. They accuse Milei’s government of protecting the interests of a privileged few while asking the rest of the country to bear the cost of his economic plan.

articles.title: L.A. County prosecutors weigh charges in Eric Swalwell case after sheriff’s investigation
articles.summary: Swalwell resigned from Congress and dropped out of the California governor’s race after multiple sexual assault and misconduct allegations, which he denies.
articles.body: The Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office sex crimes unit is weighing whether to bring charges in a case involving former Rep. Eric Swalwell, a spokesperson told NBC News on Thursday. The county sheriff’s victims’ unit investigated the case, which was then forwarded to prosecutors on Sept. 21, according to the spokesperson. Swalwell, a Democrat, resigned from Congress in April and dropped out of the California governor’s race after multiple sexual assault and misconduct allegations, which he denies. Former model and fashion software company owner Lonna Drewes held a news conference in April with her attorneys in Los Angeles, accusing Swalwell of drugging, sexually assaulting and choking her. Los Angeles authorities confirmed at the time that they had launched a criminal investigation into the allegations. An attorney for Swalwell said in an email Thursday that he is “innocent,” adding that “these allegations are false, and the facts will bear that out.” “The reported referral to the Los Angeles County District Attorney is a standard procedural step. It is not a charging decision. It is not a finding of wrongdoing. It changes nothing about the facts,” said the attorney, Sara Azari. “We welcome a fair, independent review, and we are confident it will vindicate him.” The FBI searched Swalwell’s Washington, D.C., home in August and seized an electronic device in connection with an investigation that was described as involving sexual misconduct allegations at the time, according to an official familiar with the matter. The same month, FBI agents executing a search warrant stopped Swalwell at the San Francisco airport and took his electronic devices. A copy of the search warrant obtained by NBC News detailed that investigators seized an iPhone and a MacBook Pro computer. The allegations first came to light in a San Francisco Chronicle article in which a former Swalwell aide said he had sexually assaulted her twice. A source familiar with the woman’s account confirmed to NBC News that the Chronicle’s reporting was accurate. The article was followed by a CNN report in which four women, including one whose story matched the Chronicle article, made sexual misconduct allegations against him. One of the three others, Ally Sammarco, said Swalwell sent her unsolicited photos of his penis; Sammarco later spoke to NBC News and confirmed the accuracy of her account in the CNN article. Swalwell denied the accusations published by the Chronicle and CNN in a video on social media on April 10, saying, “These allegations of sexual assault are flat false.” “They did not happen. They have never happened. And I will fight them with everything I have,” he said. Swalwell served in Congress for 13 years. A special election was held in June to fill the seat he vacated upon resignation; Democrat Aisha Wahab won the race to fill out the rest of his term. The election in November for a full two-year term will be a rematch between Wahab and fellow Democrat Melissa Hernandez.

articles.title: Massie: Trump should fire Hegseth before he is impeached
articles.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) suggested that President Trump should remove Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth from his position before the House votes to impeach him. The Kentucky Republican, who often finds himself in the crosshairs of Trump for frequently breaking with the party, was responding to a report claiming that the president was considering firing the…
articles.body:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) suggested that President Trump should remove Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth from his position before the House votes to impeach him.

The Kentucky Republican, who often finds himself in the crosshairs of Trump for frequently breaking with the party, was responding to a report claiming that the president was considering firing the Pentagon chief after the midterm election and blamed him for the unpopular Iran war.

“Trump should fire Hegseth to avoid Hegseth’s impeachment. It’s the honorable thing to do,” Massie said in response to the post on the social platform X .

House GOP leaders pushed the vote that was originally scheduled to take place in September to the lame-duck season, avoiding a controversial vote before the midterm elections took place.

Massie, along with Democrats, accused Republicans of stalling a vote that could potentially hurt the GOP’s chances in tough races in November. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) denied altering the schedule to avoid controversy in the elections, calling the accusations “ridiculous.”

“The House recessed early to avoid the vote, so I will reintroduce Hegseth articles of impeachment when we return for the lame duck session, regardless of the outcome of the midterm election,” Massie said.

Massie first unveiled his efforts to impeach Hegseth in September, accusing him of launching an illegal war in Iran without approval from Congress and said he had “abused the powers of the Department of Defense.”

He introduced articles of impeachment on the House floor, accusing Hegseth of “high crimes and misdemeanors.”

Massie had previously introduced a war powers resolution to limit Trump’s military actions in Iran amid rising death toll numbers of U.S. soldiers as fighting between the U.S. and Iran continued.

The outgoing congressman lost in Kentucky’s GOP primary this year to Trump-backed opponent Ed Gallrein.

articles.title: Zacharia confirms she did not pass bar exam
articles.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said late Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam after her legal background prior to joining the Trump administration was called into question. Zacharia, who has previously claimed to be a lawyer and was described as an “attorney” by President Trump, faced scrutiny in her first week…
articles.body:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said late Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam after her legal background prior to joining the Trump administration was called into question.

Zacharia, who has previously claimed to be a lawyer and was described as an “attorney” by President Trump, faced scrutiny in her first week on the job after she failed to answer which state she passed the bar exam required to practice law.

“You went to Pepperdine Law School but you did not pass the bar exam, correct?” Fox News host Sean Hannity asked the new press secretary in an interview.

Her legal background came into question following her shaky debut at the White House podium on Tuesday, where she was criticized for appearing nervous throughout the 14-minute press briefing and for taking questions from only three outlets.

She was later asked by reporters which state she passed the bar exam in, to which she twice replied, “When I moved to China.”

Zacharia said the reason for her bizarre answer was because she misheard the question over the noise of Marine One and did not want to break protocol by stepping in front of the president to get closer to the reporters.

Trump tapped Zacharia to replace former press secretary Karoline Leavitt, announcing her appointment on Friday — just days before her first press briefing.

Zacharia earned her law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011, but soon after moved to China for her husband’s job.

In an interview with right-wing media outlet Real America’s Voice on Thursday, Zacharia said she was registered to take the test but then decided to move to China for her husband instead of taking it.

“I didn’t want to withdraw from that, and we knew we would be moving out to China,” she said. “And after moving to China, I didn’t really think much of the bar results or consider that something that I needed to focus on.”
